title: Klingon, a language built for Star Trek
hook: A linguist built Klingon to sound alien, and fans translated Hamlet into it.
peek: Klingon began as a few lines of film dialogue and grew into a full language with its own grammar and dictionary. Its creator, the linguist Marc Okrand, deliberately broke patterns most human languages follow, and fans took it from there.
lede: For Star Trek III in 1984, Paramount asked the linguist Marc Okrand to give the Klingons a real language. He built on a handful of words the actor James Doohan had made up for an earlier film, then designed a full grammar and vocabulary. His aim was a language that would sound and work unlike anything spoken on Earth, while still being learnable.

bullets.text: Okrand chose sounds that rarely appear together in one language, including the rasping tlh and a q made far back in the throat. He mixed them so that no single Earth language would feel familiar.
Klingon puts the object first, then the verb, then the subject, an order very few human languages use. A sentence like the dog bit the man comes out roughly as man bit dog.
Okrand's Klingon Dictionary came out in 1985 and became a hit with fans. In 1992 they founded the Klingon Language Institute, which runs courses and publishes work in the language.
A film joke said you have not experienced Shakespeare until you read him in the original Klingon. The Klingon Language Institute took it seriously and published a full Klingon Hamlet in 1996.
